name: finnish-basics

description.en: 120 basic Finnish words and phrases for beginners: the numbers 0–20, the tens and 100, the days of the week, the months, eight colours, family members, greetings and polite phrases, everyday nouns, six adjectives and 16 verbs in their dictionary form (the first infinitive). The front shows the Finnish word; the back gives its English and Swedish meaning, or the digits for a number. Words come from Wikidata's lexemes and items and the US Foreign Service Institute's Conversational Finnish (public domain); meanings from Wikidata or the authors, checked against Kotus's Nykysuomen sanalista (single words), English and Swedish Wiktionary, and Folkets lexikon (the English and Swedish).
description.sv: 120 grundläggande finska ord och fraser för nybörjare: talen 0–20, tiotalen och 100, veckodagarna, månaderna, åtta färger, familjemedlemmar, hälsningar och artighetsfraser, vardagliga substantiv, sex adjektiv och 16 verb i grundform (första infinitiven). Framsidan visar det finska ordet; baksidan ger betydelsen på engelska och svenska, eller siffrorna för ett tal. Orden kommer från Wikidatas lexem och objekt och amerikanska Foreign Service Institutes Conversational Finnish (fri från upphovsrätt); betydelserna från Wikidata eller författarna, kontrollerade mot Institutet för de inhemska språkens (Kotus) Nykysuomen sanalista (enstaka ord), engelska och svenska Wiktionary samt Folkets lexikon (engelskan och svenskan).

method: Who did the work: Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.

Word list. A candidate list of 120 words and phrases for a first Finnish course was drawn up by hand from the brief's categories (numbers 0–20, the tens and 100; days; months; colours; family; greetings and polite phrases; everyday nouns; adjectives; verbs), choosing the most basic word for each concept and following the library's first French deck where the languages allow. No frequency list or textbook word list was copied.

Wikidata lexemes. SPARQL query 1 fetched every Finnish lexeme (language Q1412) whose lemma is one of 124 candidate words (the 120 cards and four alternatives: sisar, moi, terve, nähdään), with its category, senses, English and Finnish glosses and sense items (P5137). It found 82 lexemes for 79 candidates (the 78 cards that cite a lexeme, and sisar). The lexeme search (API calls 2) for the 45 candidates not found returned no Finnish lexeme with any of these lemmas, only longer Finnish words (harmaakaihi L1574405, ystävätär L1567516, vanhainkoti L1465920) and the idiom hyvää päivää kirvesvartta (L592108), none of which is the word on the card. The full JSON of the lexemes found was fetched with API calls 3, and the lexemes that their translation statements (P5972) point to with API calls 4. Where two lexemes share a lemma, both are cited (yksi: L411314 and L1567518; sisko is cited with sisar, L31796); for kaksi and neljä the numeral lexemes (L1568610, L1568611) were used.

Wikidata items. The items linked from the chosen senses, the number items 0–100 (the same items as the French deck's), and items found with the item search in Finnish and English (API calls 6 and 7: e.g. kiitos Q17249274, tervetuloa Q13109234, kyllä Q6452715, ruskea Q47071, isoisä Q9238344, isoäiti Q9235758, maito Q8495, hello Q12068060, good evening Q19279366, goodbye Q2506912) were fetched with API calls 5 (labels, aliases and descriptions in fi, en, sv and mul). They gave the Finnish word where no lexeme exists (the numbers 0 and 11–90 as fi aliases, five colours, grandparents, kiitos, tervetuloa, kyllä, milk, window, street, friend and iso as an alias of Q12935276), and the English and Swedish names of days, months, colours, family members, some greetings and everyday things. A SPARQL query for the number items by numeric value (query 8) returned nothing and was not used; the number items were taken by their ids.

Phrases from the FSI course. For the greetings and polite phrases with no Wikidata lexeme or Finnish label, the Internet Archive was searched for public-domain US Government Finnish courses (call 9). It found the Foreign Service Institute's Conversational Finnish (1987), whose textbook OCR text was downloaded (call 10). Hyvää huomenta, hyvää päivää, hyvää iltaa and tervetuloa come from the Unit I list "Greetings when meeting"; hyvää yötä, näkemiin and hei (in hei sitten) from "Greetings when departing"; ole hyvä (olkaa hyvä/ole hyvä) and anteeksi from "Other courtesy forms". In these lists the Finnish and the English are printed in separate columns, which the OCR text gives one after the other; they were read in order. Dialogue lines that give a phrase and its English on one line (Hyvää päivää. Good day.; Näkemiin, rouva Virtanen. Good bye, Mrs. Virtanen.; Kiitos kyllä … Yes, please.) were found with grep and Python scripts that print the matching lines with their context (call 11). The OCR text has no ä or ö; the spelling on the cards comes from Kotus's word list and from Wiktionary. Unit and page numbers in the evidence come from the page markers printed in the OCR text (II-47, III-20, …).

Writing the cards. The front is the Finnish word as in the lexeme's lemma, the item's Finnish label or alias, or FSI's phrase, in lower case (Finnish writes days, months and greetings in lower case). Nouns and adjectives are in the nominative singular, verbs in the first infinitive (the dictionary form). The back is the authors' own short English and Swedish rendering of the main sense: for nouns the bare noun, for verbs the infinitive (English "to …", Swedish "att …"), for numbers the digits (tagged zxx, as digits are in no language). English and Swedish follow the Wikidata labels where an item has them; otherwise they are the usual equivalents, chosen by the authors and checked in English Wiktionary, Swedish Wiktionary and Folkets lexikon. Where a Finnish word has two everyday English or Swedish equivalents both are given (poika: son, boy; käsi: hand, arm; mennä: gå, åka; hyvä: bra, god; anteeksi: excuse me, sorry). Swedish greetings are written as two words (god morgon, god dag, god kväll, god natt), as Swedish Wiktionary gives them. Rule for text not given by a content source: English and Swedish equivalents and the facts behind the notes come from the authors' own knowledge of the languages, are worded by the authors and are only confirmed in the verification sources; such single words and short facts of usage count as the authors' own content.

Notes. A short note was added where it helps a beginner and a source confirms it: kuusi also meaning spruce (with the front note "number"); the -toista and -kymmentä endings of the teens and tens (FSI's structural note on numerals); sisar beside sisko; tyttö for girl; the everyday vaari and ukki, mummo and mummu; hei when leaving; päivää for hyvää päivää; kuulemiin on the phone; kiitos kyllä; olkaa hyvä; joo and the answer by repeating the verb; ei as the negative verb; mies also meaning husband; suuri beside iso; minulla on for having; voida of health; lukea for studying; the Swedish gå and åka on mennä. Notes are the authors' own wording.

Cross-checking. Every single Finnish word was looked up in Kotus's Nykysuomen sanalista 2024 (call 13) for its spelling and word class. Every Finnish word and phrase was looked up in English Wiktionary's REST definitions (call 14, Finnish section) and in the Finnish section of Swedish Wiktionary (call 15); the first definitions are quoted in each card's evidence. Every Swedish word was checked in Folkets lexikon (call 16), English → Swedish, or Swedish → English when the first direction had no match. A Python script built the evidence lines from the responses saved during authoring, so each quote is what the source returned, with HTML, wiki markup and templates removed; quotations longer than 120 characters are cut and marked with "…". The raw responses and scripts were working files and are not published.

Dictionaries not used. The brief suggested checking the Finnish against the Kielitoimiston sanakirja. Kotus's list of open materials names the Nykysuomen sanalista, a word list built from the dictionary's headwords, as CC BY 4.0, but not the dictionary itself, and the dictionary's page on kotus.fi states no licence (it says only that the dictionary is free to use online). The dictionary was therefore not consulted; its CC BY 4.0 word list was used instead. SAOL and Svensk ordbok were not consulted either; Folkets lexikon and Swedish Wiktionary, whose licences allow automated use, verified the Swedish.

Machine checks. The dossier's Wikidata checks (the Finnish, English and Swedish label or alias of each linked item that matches the card's text, and the mul digit label of each number) are re-run against live Wikidata by the builder on every build. Wikidata lexemes cannot be checked by the builder (it checks items only); the lexeme facts in the evidence were read from the API responses of 4 October 2026. The built deck was validated with the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators (scripts/validate_sources.ts).

Excluded: nähdään (see you; Wikidata has no lexeme and FSI has it only inside a sentence), the colloquial moi and terve (FSI gives them as Hi! and Hello!, but a beginner's deck keeps hei), the colloquial joo and kiitti (named in notes, not cards), purple and orange (violetti, purppura, lila; oranssi, oranssinvärinen: several competing words), tyttö (girl, named in the note on tytär), sisar (named in the note on sisko), suuri (named in the note on iso), and tietää/tuntea (both to know).
selection: 120 cards: the cardinal numbers 0–20, the tens 30–90 and 100 (29); the seven days of the week; the twelve months; eight colours (red, blue, green, yellow, black, white, grey, brown); eight family members (mother, father, brother, sister, son or boy, daughter, grandfather, grandmother); twelve greetings and polite phrases (hei, hyvää huomenta, hyvää päivää, hyvää iltaa, hyvää yötä, näkemiin, kiitos, ole hyvä, anteeksi, tervetuloa, kyllä, ei); 22 everyday nouns (house, water, bread, milk, apple, book, table, chair, door, window, dog, cat, town, street, school, man, woman, friend, hand, day, night, week); six common adjectives (iso, pieni, hyvä, huono, uusi, vanha); and 16 common verbs in the first infinitive (olla, mennä, tulla, tehdä, puhua, syödä, juoda, rakastaa, haluta, voida, nähdä, lukea, kirjoittaa, nukkua, asua, ymmärtää). Finnish has no verb "to have" (it says minulla on, "at me is"; see the note on olla), so asua and ymmärtää take the places of the French deck's avoir and travailler. The list was chosen by the deck's authors for a first course, not copied from any frequency list or textbook. Left out: nähdään, the colloquial moi, terve, joo and kiitti, purple and orange (several competing words), tyttö, sisar and suuri (named in notes), and tietää/tuntea. All words are standard Finnish as in Kotus's word list; days and months are in lower case, as Finnish writes them.

findings.issue: The brief named the Kielitoimiston sanakirja (Kotus) for checking the Finnish and said it is CC BY 4.0 per Kotus open data.
